title: Slab-built geometric picture frame
subtitle: A rectangular clay frame with cut geometric border design
excerpt: A rectangular picture frame in air-dry clay holds a standard 10 x 15 cm print or photo. The frame border is cut from a slab and the geometric surface design is pressed in with a needle tool and ruler before drying. No kiln is needed: the frame dries at room temperature and stands with a clay kickstand attached at the back.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Slab-building method referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry. V&A open-access collection for historical ceramic frame form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit here to cut frame shapes
The joining method: roughen both clay surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, then press together
The drying stage where clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to cut and decorate cleanly
Fully air-dried and unfired; ready for surface sealing

content.text: A rectangular picture frame in air-dry clay holds a standard 10 x 15 cm print with a 3 cm border on all sides, giving an overall frame size of 16 x 21 cm. The frame is cut from a single rolled
slab

with the centre window removed; geometric scored lines form the decorative border. A clay kickstand at the back allows the frame to stand upright on a shelf. No kiln is needed: the frame dries at room temperature.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation

Roll the clay on a canvas sheet to prevent sticking. Use two 6 mm guide sticks for even thickness. Cut all shapes in one session so the frame and kickstand dry at the same rate. The frame is a single flat piece: the key risk is warping during drying, so take care with the drying setup from the start.
Rolling and cutting the frame
Roll the clay to 6 mm thick. Cut a rectangle 22 cm x 17 cm using a ruler and fettling knife. This is the outer frame shape with a small allowance for shrinkage.

Mark the centre window: measuring in 3 cm from each edge, draw a rectangle 16 cm x 11 cm on the slab surface. Cut this window out cleanly with a fettling knife held vertically. Remove the centre slab.

This frame holds a standard 10 x 15 cm print. A 3 cm border all round makes the frame 16 x 21 cm in total. Cut it from a single rolled slab. Cut out the centre window. Score lines across the border for a geometric look. Add a clay kickstand at the back. No kiln is needed. The frame dries at room temperature.
Adding the geometric border design

While the slab is still soft, lay a ruler across the frame and draw lines with a needle tool to create the geometric pattern. One repeating design that works well: two parallel lines 4 mm apart running inside the outer edge, then a row of small diagonal crosses or chevrons in the space between the lines.

This picture frame holds a standard 10 x 15 cm print. A 3 cm border on all sides gives a frame 16 x 21 cm overall. Cut the frame from a single rolled slab. Remove the centre window. Score geometric lines across the border for decoration. Add a clay kickstand at the back so it stands on a shelf. No kiln is needed. The frame dries at room temperature.
For a cross-hatch pattern: score a grid of lines 10 mm apart at 45 degrees across the border area, then repeat at 90 degrees to the first set to create diamonds.
Work lightly on the first pass: you can deepen the lines on a second pass, but you cannot erase them from wet clay.
Making and attaching the kickstand
Roll a slab strip 1 cm x 10 cm x 6 mm. This is the kickstand. Allow it to stiffen slightly on the canvas for 10 minutes.
Turn the frame face-down on a soft surface.
Score and slip

the top 2 cm of the kickstand and the corresponding area on the lower back of the frame. Press the kickstand to the frame back at a slight angle, so its free end touches the surface when the frame stands upright.

Test the stand angle immediately: prop the frame upright and check that the kickstand foot touches the surface and the frame leans at a comfortable viewing angle (roughly 70 to 80 degrees from the surface). Adjust while the clay is still soft.
Drying

Place the frame face-down on a flat board lined with paper. Cover loosely with a cloth for the first 24 hours to slow drying and prevent warping. The large flat surface of the frame is prone to drying unevenly if the top face dries faster than the bottom. After 24 hours, flip the frame face-up and allow to air-dry fully to
leather-hard
and then
bone-dry
over two to three days at room temperature.
Sealing and finishing

Sand the perimeter edges lightly with fine sandpaper for a smooth finish. Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water, allowing each coat to dry fully. For a more decorative finish, paint the geometric scored lines with a contrasting acrylic colour before sealing, using a fine liner brush to work colour into the grooves. Wipe the flat border surface clean between brush strokes to keep the colour in the lines only.
Mounting the photo

Cut a backing card from card stock slightly smaller than the overall frame, at 21 cm x 16 cm. Attach the photo to the backing card with tape. Secure the backing card to the frame back with small strips of reusable adhesive or a thin bead of PVA. The photo is viewable through the window from the front.
Use and care

This frame is a decorative indoor piece. Air-dry clay is not waterproof: keep it away from humid spaces. Dust the clay surface with a dry brush. Do not wash. The kickstand is the most fragile attachment: handle the frame by its sides.
Variations
Make a square format frame at 18 x 18 cm outer with a 12 x 12 cm window, for Instagram-format prints.
Press a pottery stamp along the border instead of scoring geometric lines by hand, for a faster repeating pattern.
Drill a small hole at the top centre of the frame at bone-dry stage and thread a cord for wall hanging, instead of using the kickstand.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Frame warps across its long axis during drying
items.cause: The top surface dried faster than the bottom, pulling the corners upward
items.fix: Dry face-down for the first 24 hours. At leather-hard, press the frame flat between two boards under light weight overnight

items.cause: The right-angle interior corners concentrate stress during drying
items.fix: Round the window corners slightly when cutting: a 3-4 mm radius at each corner relieves the stress concentration

items.problem: Kickstand breaks away from the frame back
items.cause: The score-and-slip join was not thorough, or the kickstand dried at a different rate from the frame
items.fix: Re-attach at leather-hard with fresh slip and a small clay fillet pressed into the join angle. At bone-dry, repair a broken kickstand with PVA glue

items.problem: Geometric scored lines look ragged rather than crisp
items.cause: The clay was too wet when scored, causing the needle tool to drag clay rather than cut cleanly
items.fix: Allow the slab to stiffen for 15 to 20 minutes after rolling before scoring. Wipe the needle tool clean between strokes to prevent drag
